$comment: What text a resource's bytes are, as every reader of one must read them. An offset counts the code points of this text (offset-cases.json), so two readers that make different texts of the same bytes put one annotation in two places: a reader that kept a leading byte-order mark would have every offset one further on than a reader that left it out. THE RULE. The bytes are read in the charset their content type states in its `charset` parameter, whose name and whose value are read in any case, and as UTF-8 when it states none. `iso-8859-1` and `latin1` are read as windows-1252, of which Latin-1 is a part, as a browser reads them. A byte-order mark at the very start of the bytes, when it is the mark of the encoding they are read in (EF BB BF in UTF-8, FF FE in UTF-16LE, FE FF in UTF-16BE), is not part of the text: it is left out, once. A mark anywhere else is U+FEFF, a character of the text like any other, and so is a second mark after the first. The bytes of another encoding's mark are what they are in the encoding read. A sequence the encoding does not have is U+FFFD, the replacement character, one for the sequence, and the reading goes on. A charset the reader does not decode is refused: nothing is read as something it is not, and the bytes are still there to read. A CASE is the `contentType` the bytes came with, the `bytes` in hexadecimal, two digits to a byte and a space between bytes, and either the `text` they are or `refused`: true. In this file U+FEFF and U+FFFD are written as escapes, so that each can be seen. The cases keep to charsets every runner decodes, and decodes alike: UTF-8, UTF-16LE and UTF-16BE, windows-1252 by three of its labels, and KOI8-R. Which other charsets a reader decodes, and under which names, is not held here. RUN BY TypeScript in packages/core (decode-cases.test.ts) against `decodeWithCharset`, by which the TypeScript SDK and the Browser read a resource's text, and against `decodeRepresentation`, by which the Smelter and the Librarian do; by the Rust SDK (tests/decode_cases.rs) and by the Python SDK (tests/test_decode_cases.py), each through its client's `browse.resource_content`, by which a worker reads the text it counts offsets in. The Rust SDK decodes UTF-8 alone without its `charsets` feature and refuses every other charset; it runs these cases with the feature. A reader in another language runs them too. Add a case here before changing a reader.

cases.why: a content type that states no charset: the bytes are UTF-8, and a character outside the basic plane is one character
a charset stated in capitals is the charset it is in lower case
a leading byte-order mark is not part of the text
a leading mark is left out where no charset is stated too
a mark that is not leading is a character of the text
two marks at the start: the first is left out, and the second is a character of the text
cases.bytes: ef bb bf ef bb bf 78

cases.why: nothing but a mark is the empty text
a byte UTF-8 does not have is U+FFFD, and the reading goes on
a sequence cut short is one U+FFFD, not one for each of its bytes
iso-8859-1 is read as windows-1252, as a browser reads it: 93 and 94 are quotation marks, not controls
latin1 is the same encoding by another name, and the parameter needs no space before it
the parameter's own name is read in any case, and other parameters may follow it
UTF-8's mark is no mark in windows-1252: its three bytes are three characters of the text
UTF-16LE: its leading mark is left out
UTF-16LE: a mark that is not leading is a character of the text
UTF-16LE: a character outside the basic plane is two units and one character
UTF-16BE: its leading mark is left out
another charset, stated in capitals: KOI8-R
cases.bytes: d0 d2 c9 d7 c5 d4

cases.why: a charset no reader decodes is refused, and nothing is read as UTF-8 in its place
